body: A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any further sign that housing is cooling faster than the central bank expects. Bank stocks face slower mortgage growth, especially in investor lending, which has traditionally been a profitable segment. With energy-driven inflation still the RBA’s main worry, oil prices remain the swing factor for whether housing weakness is enough to keep rates on hold. Tax changes, lending caps and five rate hikes have all hit Australian property investors at once, and the result is a collapse in landlord borrowing. The value of new Australian home loans fell 15.5% in the September quarter, nearly twice the 8% decline economists had expected, as lending to property investors collapsed in the wake of government tax changes and a year of Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes. Investor lending was the main drag, plunging 32.3% on the quarter after a 10.2% fall in the June quarter. Owner-occupier loan values fell a more modest 5.3%, following a 1.9% decline previously. The overall drop was a sharp acceleration from the 5.2% fall recorded in the prior quarter. The split between investors and owner-occupiers suggests policy is doing much of the work. In the May federal budget, the government moved to end negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night, keeping it only for newly built properties, and also announced curbs to the capital gains tax discount on established dwellings. Negative gearing lets investors offset rental losses against other income. The government argued the housing market needed rebalancing, with most investor credit going towards existing homes rather than new supply. The major banks moved quickly to reflect the changes in how they assess investor loan applications, reducing borrowing capacity for many landlords. Those measures came on top of tighter lending rules. From February, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority required banks to limit new loans at six or more times a borrower’s income to 20% of new mortgage lending, measured separately for owner-occupiers and investors. Monetary policy has added further pressure. The RBA has raised its cash rate five times this year, in February, March, May, September and November, taking it to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, as it fights inflation that has been pushed higher by energy costs. The November decision was split 6-3, and the statement dropped earlier language about further increases. The RBA’s own November Statement on Monetary Policy had already flagged a steep fall in investor lending, describing the drop in investor loan commitments as the largest in any hiking cycle on record. Governor Michele Bullock said a pullback in investor demand was normal in a housing downturn. The bigger fall compared with owner-occupiers, though, suggests the budget changes are having an effect. The figures strengthen the case that housing is cooling quickly, which may feed into the RBA’s assessment of whether its tightening has gone far enough. body: The broad-based jump in confidence, especially among service firms, adds to the picture of a Japanese economy strong enough to cope with higher interest rates. Combined with the reported tight labour market and persistent cost pressure, that could support expectations of further Bank of Japan tightening, which would be supportive for the yen. For equities, the strength in electronics and precision machinery reinforces the chip-led earnings story behind Japan’s tech and equipment names. The caution on passing costs on to customers is a reminder that margin pressure has not gone away. Japan Inc’s mood is at multi-year highs on chips and services, even as rising prices and borrowing costs start to pinch. Japanese manufacturers’ confidence climbed to its highest level in more than five years in November, lifted by booming semiconductor demand, while sentiment among non-manufacturers reached its strongest in over eight years, according to the Reuters Tankan poll. The manufacturers’ index rose to +27 from +22 in October, its highest reading since August 2021. The non-manufacturers’ index surged to +35 from +23, a level last seen in June 2018. The monthly poll is closely watched as a leading indicator for the Bank of Japan’s quarterly Tankan business survey. It was conducted from October 27 to November 6, and 214 of the 508 firms surveyed responded. Readings are calculated by subtracting the percentage of pessimistic responses from optimistic ones, so a positive figure signals net optimism. Chipmakers and their suppliers drove the gain among manufacturers. Sentiment in electronics jumped to +39 from +25, with one respondent describing demand for semiconductors, particularly memory chips, as very strong. Precision machinery, which includes some chip equipment makers, improved to +42 from +38 on robust domestic and overseas orders. Another machinery firm said shipments to the semiconductor market had reached unprecedented levels. Oil refining and ceramics rose to +25 from +14, while chemicals improved to +33 from +27. The service side of the economy was just as upbeat. Information and communications sentiment rose to +29 from +8 on strong orders, while services and others more than doubled to +43 from +19. One manager pointed to persistently tight labour market conditions keeping demand for staff high. Not everything was positive. Firms in both sectors said rising prices and higher interest rates were weighing on business, and some reported difficulty passing increased costs on to customers. Looking ahead, manufacturers expect sentiment to edge up to +28 in February, while non-manufacturers see confidence easing to +29, still well above recent levels. For the Bank of Japan, the combination of strong business confidence, a tight labour market and cost pressures will be one input as it weighs the outlook for policy. Its own quarterly Tankan will be the next major read on corporate sentiment. There's always something new to learn about the markets. Middle Eastern benchmarks have been weakening for weeks, suggesting an oil glut may be building amid rebounding Persian Gulf exports and global demand destruction amid high prices. On the face of it, an oversupply of crude oil could be forming. But the costs to refiners and consumers are not falling. War, insurance premiums, and record tanker rates have raised the cost of transporting a barrel of crude oil from about $5 per barrel before the war to as much as $30 a barrel, and at times even higher. Middle Eastern producers are forced to slash their official selling prices to win customers because the surge in Persian Gulf exports is weakening the physical prices of local grades. Moreover, amid high freight costs, Middle East’s crude oil could only win Asia’s price-sensitive buyers with lower prices. The pricing of the Middle Eastern barrels and the weakening market structure of the benchmark Middle East crudes signal an oil glut is forming. But the shock to the global oil and fuel markets isn’t over as increased flows don’t mean traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has suddenly become less dangerous. In fact, attacks on vessels have intensified in the past month, while producers are tying up a large portion of the global tanker fleet on inefficient shuttle movements in and out of the Strait and subsequent ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Normal oil trade patterns from before the Iran war may never return. Until the market adapts to the new normal and Gulf producers build alternative supply routes, the war and insurance premium risks will remain with crude flows. South Sudan is courting fresh capital for 14 exploration blocks and a production increase from roughly 170,000 barrels per day to 230,000, which investors would find impossible to control once those barrels left the country. Captive to neighboring Sudan’s civil war, South Sudan is essentially divvying up its oil, under duress, between the Sudanese Army and the rival paramilitary RSF, which extract payment before the oil can reach the Red Sea. The government-backed South Sudan Oil & Power conference will put that proposition before investors in Juba at the end of the month, and its organizers place current production at 170,000 barrels per day, describing 230,000 bpd as a short-term target. A petroleum ministry official reported production of 175,000 bpd in August and set a lower target of 200,000 bpd by August 2027. Tanker tracking recorded eight cargoes carrying 4.8 million barrels from Sudan’s two Red Sea terminals in October, equivalent to combined Sudanese and South Sudanese exports of 155,000 bpd . Sudan’s Heglig fields were producing about 26,000 bpd in September, all of it sent for export, according to Sudan Tribune . Public data provide no current country breakdown and no reconciliation between South Sudan’s reported wellhead production and the volumes loaded at the Red Sea terminals. Juba’s lofty ambitions in the middle of the civil war in Sudan, which has effectively hijacked its exports, are an attempt to ride the tailwinds of the launch of the Africa Energy Bank. Afreximbank and the African Petroleum Producers’ Organisation formally established the institution in Abuja on October 31 with $5 billion in authorized capital . APPO Secretary-General Farid Ghezali said the bank had raised $500 million for deployment and would begin making investment decisions. Fresh capital can finance production inside South Sudan, but it can’t secure passage through Sudan. Crude from Blocks 1, 2 and 4 enters the Greater Nile pipeline through Heglig in West Kordofan, where Sudan’s paramilitary RSF displaced the Sudanese Army in December 2025. A tripartite agreement placed security inside the complex with the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces. South Sudanese troops now protect the installation, while the RSF dominates the surrounding territory and the Sudanese Army controls the Red Sea terminals at the other end of the line. A September report citing unnamed oil-industry sources says Juba gives the RSF $4 of the $11 charged on each South Sudanese barrel crossing territory under its control. The army-aligned government receives the remaining $7. South Sudan has previously settled pipeline obligations with crude , although no published account identifies whether the RSF’s current share is delivered in oil, cash or export proceeds. The Army’s portion provides more than compensation for operating a pipeline. Janes assesses that Sudanese processing and transit fees provide revenue used to sustain Army operations. The RSF collects its share in exchange for allowing the crude to cross territory it controls. Investors financing production connected to Heglig would add barrels to a trade that pays both forces. South Sudan’s second export line avoids Heglig, but doesn’t escape the war. The Petrodar pipeline carries Dar Blend from Blocks 3 and 7 at Paloch through six pumping stations in Sudan to the Bashair terminal on the Red Sea. COP 31, the latest iteration of the United Nations’ annual climate conference, kicked off today in Antalya, Türkiye, and achieving 35 percent global electrification by 2035 is going to be one of the event’s most central agenda items. Until extremely recently, this target likely would have seemed overly ambitious, but experts say that a number of factors, including volatile oil and gas markets stemming from the war in Iran, paired with enormous advances in clean energy technologies, have now put that goal within “striking distance.” All of that electrification is going to require a whole lot of lithium. Over the course of this decade alone, lithium demand has already skyrocketed by more than 400 percent on a global scale to top 1.5 million metric tons per year. Projecting out to 2035, the year featured in COP 31’s proposed electrification pledge, global demand could reach approximately 4 million tons. In the International Energy Agency’s Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 , no mineral is expected to see bigger demand growth. This is leading to increased competition over global lithium supply chains as nations rush to shore up their own future supplies to ensure long-term energy security in a rapidly changing energy landscape. But even as a diverse array of countries try to establish homegrown lithium production and refining sectors, one nation is expected to maintain an extreme degree of control over global supplies: China. Beijing controls an estimated 72 percent of the global lithium-ion market, and Chinese companies control a quarter of the world’s lithium mining capacity . This control runs up the supply chain as well: in 2024, more than 80 percent of battery cells on the planet were made in China, raising major concerns about geopolitical precarity and market resilience in clean energy supply chains. By 2030, Beijing is expected to control 39 percent of the world’s lithium production, according to a recent report from Wood Mackenzie. “Lithium production and lithium ownership are increasingly diverging, and it is reshaping the global critical mineral supply chains,” said Allan Pedersen, research director, energy transition & battery materials – lithium at Wood Mackenzie. “While production growth is becoming more geographically diverse, ownership remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies, mostly led by China.” By comparison, the United States produces just barely over 1 percent of the world’s lithium supplies, a large share of which comes from a single mine: Albemarle’s Silver Peak mine in Nevada. body: API Shows Sharp Build in US Crude Oil, Distillate Inventories Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated that crude oil inventories in the United States rose by 9.0 million barrels in the week ending November 6. In the week prior, US crude oil inventories fell by 5.267 million barrels. Commercial crude oil inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 54 million barrels over the last 30 weeks, and 3 million over this year, according to API data, which has been kept in check in part thanks to draws from the SPR. For the week ending November 6, 2.7 million barrels of crude oil left the SPR to aid commercial inventories, bringing the total inventory held in the SPR down to 279.5 million barrels —a level that is 434 million barrels shy of maximum capacity. The generally accepted operational minimum for oil in the SPR is between 250-300 million barrels, below which the reserve may find it difficult to pump and process oil efficiently. title: American Barrick files for proposed IPO
summary: Barrick Mining announced Tuesday that its planned new publicly listed company will be named American Barrick Gold Corporation.
body: Barrick Mining (NYSE:B)(TSX:ABX) announced Tuesday that its planned new publicly listed company, which will hold Barrick’s North American gold assets, will be named American Barrick Gold Corporation. The world’s third-biggest gold miner said it is moving forward with the proposed initial public offering (IPO) and has filed a registration statement on Form S-11 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in connection with the proposed IPO. American Barrick intends to apply to list its common stock on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol ‘ABGC’. The number of shares to be offered and the proposed price range for the IPO have not yet been determined, the company said, adding that net proceeds from the IPO will be distributed to Barrick, which it expects to return to its shareholders. In September, chief executive officer Mark Hill said the planned North American gold IPO could slip into January. Hill, who was named in August to lead the North American unit after it goes public, said there had been “some delays” in working through formalities ahead of the listing. Barrick first announced last year its proposal to hive off its US assets from its sprawling portfolio in riskier countries. The new company will house Barrick’s joint-venture interests and the Fourmile discovery in the state of Nevada, which it has touted as “one of the century’s greatest gold discoveries.” Barrick struck a deal with Newmont in August that gave the Denver-based company a stake in Fourmile and brought the deposit into the joint Nevada Gold Mines venture in exchange for support of the planned IPO. This is reflected in technical analysis of oil price movements. Technical analysts use historical price charts to forecast market direction. One indicator they monitor in a declining market is the support level, which represents a price threshold that could act as a floor against further declines. Previous highs and lows often serve as support areas. Moving averages also play a role, smoothing out the impact of extreme fluctuations to reveal the underlying market trend. In addition, analysts use Fibonacci retracement, a percentage-based calculation to identify price levels that markets often retest after a particular move. One key Fibonacci level is now serving as a reference point for global oil prices, tracked through Brent crude futures contracts. The recent decline in oil prices briefly stalled around the 50% retracement level of the rally from July to October. According to LSEG data, this level stands at USD 94.07 per barrel and has now become an important support area. The level is also reinforced by the 200-day moving average at around USD 93.84 and the 40-week moving average at USD 95.27. After a sharp decline, markets typically pause to digest the move. This is known as consolidation and is often viewed as a healthy development within a trend. To assess the likelihood of further market declines, technical analysts use several momentum and volatility indicators. One is the Relative Strength Index (RSI), which measures momentum based on the duration and magnitude of price movements. Another is the Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD), which compares two moving averages to measure momentum. Analysts also use Bollinger Bands, which measure price deviations from a central moving average to gauge volatility. title: Mortgage rates jump sharply higher, after easing for four straight weeks. Here's why
summary: After falling for a month, mortgage rates jumped sharply higher on a hotter-than-expected inflation report.
body: Mortgage rates fell for four straight weeks, but that ended Tuesday, after a monthly inflation report came in hotter than expected. The average rate on the 30-year fixed mortgage rose 12 basis points from Monday to 7.30%, according to Mortgage News Daily. It was the largest one-day jump in more than a month. The consumer price index showed broad upward pressure on prices, not just fuel-related costs. This came after a monthly employment report Friday that also showed a more heated economy than analysts had predicted. "Given that the Fed explicitly said it was more focused on the inflation component of its job description at the moment (as opposed to the 'full employment' component), we were expecting today's data to carry far more weight than last week's jobs report. The reaction was logical an immediate," wrote Matthew Graham, chief operating officer at Mortgage News Daily. This jump comes after a monthlong reprieve in interest rates that finally brought mortgage demand back. Last week, mortgage applications rose 6.2% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. That's because last week, on a weekly average from the MBA, the rate on the 30-year fixed had decreased to 7.21% from 7.30%, for loans with a 20% down payment. That was the fourth straight weekly decline and the lowest rate since mid-September. As a result, applications to refinance a home loan rose 5% last week from the previous week but were still 57% lower than the same week one year ago. "Moreover, the FHA rate was back below 7 percent and was more than 20 basis points lower than the conforming rate, which helped first-time home buyers currently in the market," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA. CNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox. Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home rose 8% for the week but were 18% lower year over year. The share of applications for adjustable-rate mortgages also fell slightly as interest rates eased up. ARM loans offer lower rates but at higher risk. They become more popular as rates rise and borrowers seek savings. "The declining trend in rates helped to spur stronger application activity, although the pace of purchase and refinance applications remain considerably lower than a year ago. Applications for conventional, VA, and FHA purchase applications saw gains over the week, with particularly strong growth for FHA and VA loans," added Kan.

Since the start of November, Brent had lost about 21% and WTI about 17% on bets that the war was winding down. Iran’s top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, denied that talks with Washington are under way and called reports of a recent meeting in Qatar “pure lies” spread to push down oil prices. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the U.S. of conducting diplomacy through threats, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected Iran’s demand for war reparations. UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo pointed to “fading hopes of an imminent de-escalation.” Bloomberg columnist Javier Blas called Brent at around $90 “an oddity,” too low if the U.S. and Iran escalate and too high if they sign a deal. A deal would not restore Gulf flows quickly. LSEG Oil Research said traffic through Hormuz would depend on mine clearing, insurance costs and shipowners’ willingness to take the risk. Attackers struck 37 ships in October, the most in any month since the war began, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. However, a declining valuation does not necessarily mean the stock is cheap. Even as the stock price falls, Wall Street still maintains high expectations for the company's future earnings; if AI capital expenditures, data center construction, or profit margins fall short of forecasts, the currently seemingly cheap valuation could rise rapidly. The forward P/E ratio is determined jointly by stock price and future earnings expectations. Nvidia's stock price has recently pulled back sharply, but analysts have not yet lowered their profit forecasts for the next 12 months in tandem, leading to a rapid decline in its valuation multiple. There are two possible explanations for this situation. One is that market sentiment is overly pessimistic, with the stock price having already priced in slowing AI spending as well as regulatory and corporate governance risks ahead of time, while actual earnings could still continue to grow. The energy and water needs of the AI sector are growing larger all the time, placing enormous pressure on the world’s finite resources and putting unprecedented strain on global energy grids. There is no closing Pandora’s box: AI is here to stay. So how do we change its functionality to keep its operations and growth projections within planetary boundaries? Some experts say that quantum computing could hold the key. According to figures from the International Energy Agency, global electricity generation to supply data centres is expected to grow from 460 terawatt hours (TWh) in 2024 to over 1,000 TWh in 2030, and then 1,300 TWh in 2035. That’s the equivalent of adding a whole other Germany to the global power demand by 2024. Under this scenario, by 2030 the world’s data centers alone will be consuming more than all of Russia – the fourth largest energy consumer in the world at 1,176.11 TWh per year. "One of the reasons the next generations of AI are looking to consume so much power is that a whole class of the problems they are solving are problems that really are much better suited to quantum calculations," Andrew Dzurak, founder of an Australian quantum startup called Diraq, recently told AFP. Quantum technologies aren’t yet ready for real-world application, but Dzurak says they will be in just a handful of years. His company is currently conducting the world's first field test of a quantum computer in a data center application in Sydney. Building on that work, Dzurak says that quantum computing is already evolving out of lab settings and “will be ready to lift the burden in data centers within five years” according to Phys.org. To be sure, quantum computing requires a significant amount of energy to run, and most models require extremely cold cryogenic temperatures to run. However, that energy demand pales in comparison to the amount of energy needed by the hyperscale data centers currently powering the AI boom. Echoing Dzurak’s sentiments, a September report by nonpartisan global news outlet Semafor stated that “ the sector’s carbon footprint will be relatively small compared to the AI industry’s because quantum is more likely to be used to address specific problems rather than as a general purpose technology.” What is more, quantum computing could make artificial intelligence itself more energy efficient by changing the way that large language models function. “For the things that quantum computing is good at — such as AI processing — there's no way for any GPU to compete against us. body: Pro-Palestinian activists who pressured Eni and Dana Petroleum to quit an Israeli offshore gas venture are now going after Murphy Oil, the Houston-based company that replaced them on Monday. The Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement and its partners called on Murphy on Wednesday to give up the six Zone G exploration licenses it holds 50-50 with Israel’s Ratio Energies. The licenses cover about 1,700 square kilometers of seabed near the Leviathan gas field, and Murphy is the operator. Israel awarded Zone G in October 2023 to Eni, Ratio and Aberdeen-based Dana, a subsidiary of state-run Korea National Oil Corporation. Eni withdrew earlier this year , citing a reallocation of investments, and Israeli financial daily Globes reported that pro-Palestinian pressure also made the company reluctant to enter Israel. Israel’s Energy Ministry announced Dana’s exit on Monday, according to Korea’s Yonhap news agency. Dana had faced protests in Aberdeen and a complaint to South Korea’s Board of Audit and Inspection. According to the civic group that filed the complaint, the board closed the case after finding that the licensing process had stopped and that Dana plans to withdraw . Dana and KNOC have not commented. Israeli media have reported that Dana can rejoin with regulatory approval. Campaigners in Scotland, South Korea and Italy claimed both exits as wins and urged investors, insurers and contractors to stay out of the project. They argue that part of Zone G overlaps the maritime boundaries Palestine declared in 2019, which Israel does not recognize. They also cite a July 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel’s exploitation of natural resources in the occupied territories unlawful. “Murphy Oil, which has now taken the place Dana and Eni abandoned, should expect exactly the same treatment,” said Dave Black of the Scottish Palestine Solidarity Campaign. Murphy has not responded publicly to the campaign. On Wednesday, it announced four production sharing contracts covering about 2.6 million acres offshore Cameroon. Murphy and Ratio have 36 months to drill an exploration well in Zone G. Ratio also holds 15% of Leviathan, which supplies Egypt under a $35 billion export contract. body: The leading economics blog online covering financial issues, geopolitics and trading. The story in the Strait of Hormuz has been that Middle Eastern crude exports have recovered to about 80% to 85% of pre-war levels, including pipeline shipments, while refined-product exports remain muted. The uneven recovery shows how Gulf producers prioritize crude oil shipments over refined products as the Hormuz chokepoint remains vulnerable despite encouraging diplomatic signals . Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of industry consultant FGE NexantECA, said last week that while Middle Eastern crude exports, including pipeline shipments, have recovered to 80% to 85% of pre-war levels, refined-product shipments remain at around 35% to 40%. "Oil infrastructure such as refineries remains susceptible to drone strikes," which has led Gulf producers to prioritize crude shipments, said Xavier Tang, senior market analyst for Vortexa. More good news from Hormuz on Tuesday , as Bloomberg reports that Qatar's liquefied natural gas loadings have reached 13 to 15 shipments per 10-day period on a moving-average basis this month, up from about 11 in October, or roughly half of pre-war levels. The figures are based on Bloomberg, Kpler and Copernicus data. A pickup in Qatari LNG supply reaching the global market would be welcome news for Europe, where natural gas inventories are well below seasonal norms and gas prices trade around 82 euros per megawatt-hour, down from more than 100 euros before last week's positive diplomatic signals erased a hefty war-risk premium in energy markets. One of Qatar's LNG tankers was attacked last month, but that hasn't decreased exports or Hormuz transits. Previous attacks slowed Qatari LNG flows through Hormuz. These positive developments toward ending the conflict and easing the global energy crisis sound promising, but stockpiles worldwide have been dangerously depleted this year . Ukraine's relentless targeting of Russian refineries suggests that global markets will remain tight well into next year, especially for diesel. For Europe, the window to rebuild NatGas inventories has closed, with seasonal storage withdrawals already underway for several weeks. As we reported Monday, Qatar is hedging against what could be years of Hormuz chokepoint uncertainty with deals to buy up to 7 million tons of US LNG annually from Cheniere and Woodside. This year's US-Iran conflict knocked out roughly 17% of Qatar's export capacity, costing an estimated $20 billion in annual revenue. With deliveries beginning in 2030 and 2031, the deals cement America's LNG dominance into the 2030s and reveal a striking reversal: one of the world's largest LNG exporters is turning to its biggest rival for insurance amid Hormuz uncertainty that will linger for years. title: Minerals 260 lines up A$410M for gold project
summary: The backing advances a potential 150,000-oz.-a-year producer near Kalgoorlie, while leaving the construction decision for 2027.
body: Minerals 260 (ASX: MI6) has secured A$410 million (C$399 million) in bank debt for its Bullabulling gold project in Western Australia, with no requirement to lock in future gold prices. ANZ, National Australia Bank and Société Générale have committed A$335 million for project financing and A$75 million for working capital. Together with equity and Franco-Nevada (TSX: FNV; NYSE: FNV) royalty funding, the package would cover development through first production, Minerals 260 said Wednesday. Securing credit approval before completing the feasibility study reflects “the high quality, high margin and long-life aspects of Bullabulling,” Managing Director Luke McFadyen said in the release. The backing advances a potential 150,000-oz.-a-year producer near Kalgoorlie, while leaving the construction decision and final loan conditions due early next year. Bullabulling could begin producing in the second half of 2028, Franco-Nevada said in September. Financing conditions include completing the definitive feasibility study, final due diligence, loan documents and an agreement with Franco-Nevada governing creditors’ rights. The first debt drawdown is expected late next year. The project loan runs for seven years and working capital financing for four. Interest is less than three percentage points above Australia’s bank bill swap bid rate — equivalent to below about 8% annually using the current three-month benchmark. The company hasn’t disclosed the exact margin or benchmark term. Interest accrued during construction will be added to the debt. BMO Capital Markets initiated coverage on Nov. 10 with an outperform rating and a A$1.75 share-price target. That is nearly twice Wednesday’s closing price of A88¢, a 3.5% gain, valuing the company at about A$2.25 billion. The shares have traded between about A29¢ and A$1 over the past year. Franco-Nevada agreed in September to provide another $170 million in royalty funding and buy $30 million of Minerals 260 shares. That brought its aggregate backing to $420 million and increased its gross royalty on Bullabulling to 3.9% from 2.45%. July’s prefeasibility study envisaged annual output averaging about 150,000 oz. over the first decade and a 19-year operating life. The initial processing plant would handle 5 million tonnes annually, with provision for expansion, Franco-Nevada said. Bullabulling, 65 km from Kalgoorlie, has 140 million indicated tonnes at 0.98 gram per tonne gold for 4.4 million oz., plus 51 million inferred tonnes at 1 gram gold for 1.7 million oz., according to a resource issued in July. The backing advances a potential 150,000-oz.-a-year producer near Kalgoorlie, while leaving the construction decision for 2027.

title: Troilus hits gold in Quebec ground marked as waste
summary: The exploration work comes as Troilus assembles financing for a redevelopment on the site of a former gold-copper mine.
body: Troilus Mining (TSX: TLG; US-OTC: CHXMF) has found gold in past-producing ground treated as waste at its namesake Quebec project, raising the prospect of improving the planned open-pit operation’s economics. Hole 87-26-524 cut 34 metres at 1.29 grams gold per tonne from 207 metres depth, including 12 metres at 3.04 grams, Troilus said Wednesday . The results come from the Z87 hanging wall, beside the main mineralized zone. “We view the results positively, as they support potential resource conversion, lower strip ratios, improved early-year mill feed and future pit optimization,” Desjardins Capital Markets mining analyst Bryce Adams said Wednesday in a note. The exploration work comes as Troilus assembles financing for a redevelopment on the site of a former gold-copper mine. The federal assessment registry places the project about 170 km north of Chibougamau and 615 km north of Montreal. Converting waste to ore could reduce stripping and improve early mill feed. The results still need modelling, since the resource and reserve underlying September’s updated study exclude all 2026 drilling, Troilus said. “We are confident in our existing mine plan, but remain committed to continual improvement and evaluating opportunities to strengthen it,” CEO Justin Reid said. Some historical drill core was never assayed, leaving gaps in the geological model. Troilus is testing those intervals and inferred material around the proposed pit. Estimated true thicknesses are 75%–90% of the reported drill lengths. September’s development update for the project envisaged a 26-year operation, with construction anticipated in 2027, first ore in September 2029 and commercial production in March 2030. Initial capital was estimated at about $1.43 billion (C$2 billion), Troilus said. Troilus received a credit-approved commitment for $850 million in debt from KfW IPEX-Bank and Société Générale in September. The package contemplated a further $250 million from Export Development Canada, subject to that lender’s final approvals, Troilus said at the time. Shares of Troilus dropped 2.8% to C$1.56 Wednesday afternoon in Toronto, valuing the company at about C$880 million ($629 million). The stock has traded between C$1.20 and C$2.47 in the past year. title: Altius to buy TNR Gold in $86-million royalty deal
summary: The mining royalty company will acquire TNR's royalties, including three projects in Argentina.
body: Altius Minerals (TSX: ALS) agreed to buy TNR Gold (TSXV: TNR) in a deal valued at C$122 million ($86 million) that boosts the company’s exposure to Argentine copper and lithium while spinning out an Alaska gold project. Each eligible TNR share would receive 0.0072 Altius shares and a quarter-share in a new company holding the Shotgun gold project, Altius said Wednesday in a statement . The package’s estimated value of 48¢ includes 38¢ in Altius stock and 10¢ assigned to the spinout, representing a 60% premium to TNR’s 30¢ close Tuesday. The acquisition fits Altius’s strategy of accumulating royalties on long-life mineral deposits. It combines potential future copper revenue from TNR’s royalty on McEwen Copper’s Los Azules project with exposure to Mariana, an operating lithium brine project where Altius already holds a royalty. TNR’s interests also include a royalty on properties within the Josemaria copper-gold project. Los Azules “represents the primary long-term opportunity, while Mariana offers nearer-term cash flow potential,” TD Securities mining analyst Craig Hutchison said in a note. Hutchison expects limited near-term financial impact from the relatively small deal, with its value dependent on development timelines at Los Azules and Josemaria. The companies’ relationship deepened in May, when Altius completed a $4.2-million investment for a minority stake and secured first-offer rights over TNR’s principal royalties. By October, Altius owned about 13% of TNR, which disclosed an unsolicited takeover proposal and entered exclusive talks. TNR’s effective interests include a 0.36% net smelter return royalty on Los Azules and 1.35% on Mariana, excluding portions held for another shareholder. Los Azules, in San Juan province, is owned by McEwen Copper, whose investors include McEwen (TSX: MUX; NYSE: MUX), Rio Tinto (ASX: RIO; LSE: RIO; NYSE: RIO) and automaker Stellantis. A 2025 feasibility study for the project outlines average annual production of about 148,200 tonnes of copper cathode over 21 years, with cash costs of US$1.71 per lb. The proposed operation would produce finished copper using heap leaching and solvent extraction-electrowinning, avoiding a conventional concentrator and reliance on outside smelters. Nearby exploration targets could eventually help extend the project’s operating life. Los Azules “offers the potential for decades of increased copper exposure within our portfolio,” Altius CEO Brian Dalton said Wednesday. McEwen Copper secured a US$240-million loan in August for engineering and early works. Full project financing and a final investment decision are targeted for mid-2027, with commercial production starting in 2030, subject to financing and approvals. That leaves the royalty’s copper cash flow dependent on successful development. At Mariana, Ganfeng Lithium inaugurated a 20,000-tonne-per-year lithium chloride plant in February 2025. The acquisition would consolidate Altius’s exposure to the operation, although TNR’s royalty carries a buyback provision: Ganfeng’s subsidiary can purchase 0.9 percentage points of TNR’s effective interest for $900,000, reducing it to 0.45%. Shotgun would remain with former TNR shareholders through the spinout. Altius would retain a 0.5% royalty and invest $2.2 million to increase its spinout ownership to just under 20%, while providing technical support. Closing of the TNR acquisition is expected around the first quarter of 2027, subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approvals. Shareholders controlling about 28% of TNR have signed support agreements; a vote is expected in December. TNR shares closed Tuesday at 30¢ in Toronto, valuing the company at $73 million, before trading was halted Wednesday morning pending news. Altius was 3.5% weaker at $51.14 Wednesday, valuing it at $3 billion. The backing advances a potential 150,000-oz.-a-year producer near Kalgoorlie, while leaving the construction decision for 2027.

title: Scorpio hits gold beyond Nevada resource
summary: The resource covering Goldwedge and the Manhattan pit areas holds 18.34 million inferred tonnes at 1.26 grams gold.
body: Scorpio Gold (TSXV, Nasdaq: SGLD) has hit high-grade gold 850 metres from the core resource area at its Manhattan project in Nevada, opening a new target for drilling beyond the ground that has anchored its exploration program. Drill hole 26MN-133 at April Fool cut 13.05 metres at 9.4 grams gold per tonne from 78.63 metres depth, the company said Tuesday. It is the target’s first deep diamond drill hole in a systematic program. “That opens the potential to extend the mineralized system well beyond the current resource footprint,” CEO Zayn Kalyan said in the statement. The result gives Scorpio a target beyond Manhattan’s existing gold inventory. Further holes must establish its size and continuity: the latest intersection does not demonstrate continuous mineralization across the 850-metre gap, and its true width remains unknown. Manhattan covers about 4,780 hectares in Nevada’s Walker Lane mineral belt, 53 km north-northeast of Tonopah and roughly four hours by road from Las Vegas. Scorpio owns the district outright, including Goldwedge and four former open pits acquired from Kinross Gold (TSX: K; NYSE: KGC) in 2021. The June 2025 resource covering Goldwedge and the Manhattan pit areas holds 18.34 million inferred tonnes at 1.26 grams gold, containing 740,000 ounces. Historical estimates covering April Fool and other satellite areas are excluded from that current resource. Earlier exploration at April Fool included reverse-circulation drilling used for a 1997 estimate, but detailed drill logs, collar coordinates and assay records have not survived, Scorpio said. The target is historical exploration ground now being tested with new core drilling. Scorpio’s broader program targets at least 50,000 metres of drilling across Manhattan. The district’s past-producing operations, historical drilling database and existing water rights provide a starting point for testing extensions and additional targets. Scorpio’s American depositary shares rose 0.8% stronger to $3.38 (C$4.73) Tuesday morning on Nasdaq, valuing the company at about $58 million. Analysis: Is Nvidia too big to fail? Its AI financing web raises the stakes
summary: The tech giant's web of ties to other companies is raising the possibility that it could do far-reaching economic and financial damage.
body: The swirl of sex-and-spying allegations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is raising a worrying question: Could trouble at the chipmaker spread through the tightly connected financial network Nvidia has built to support the artificial intelligence boom? Serious problems with Nvidia could do far-reaching economic and financial damage. The company has made hundreds of billions of dollars in financial commitments to other firms to help the industry grow, earning it the nickname the "central bank of AI." The Federal Reserve and other financial institutions are closely watching the AI buildout to monitor for the possibility that an unexpected event could destabilize the global financial system. Even back in July Fed officials were discussing the possibility of of a "broad-based repricing of assets" in the event of problems in the AI sector. A rerun of the 2007-2008 financial crisis isn't likely, according to analysts and current and former financial officials. Nvidia isn't "too big to fail in a bank sense at all," said Sheila Bair, a former government regulator who ran the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. Unlike a troubled bank, Nvidia isn't vulnerable to a sudden loss of confidence and would still produce a product customers want to buy even if something went wrong. And its massive equity gives it a cushion. But regulators need to watch carefully for exposure by the banks and the wider financial system to Nvidia and other firms like it, Bair said. "Nvidia going down would be a pretty seismic event," she said. Investors still have high hopes for Nvidia, which reports earnings on Tuesday. Analysts expect its revenue to more than double in the current fiscal year, and then to roughly double again over the following two years, according to LSEG data. But with Huang under scrutiny by the FBI, Congress, and Nvidia's board over his relationship with a woman who The New York Times reported was suspected of spying for China, analysts see a wide range of outcomes as suddenly possible, including the potential removal of Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993. The company didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Nvidia's board has expressed confidence in its CEO. Nvidia's stock fell 30% from its Oct. 6 peak through Tuesday's close, amid a broader reassessment of the AI trade prompted by Democrats' surprising victory in the Nov. 3 midterms. Its stock recovered Wednesday, rising more than 4% as of midday. Still, people who closely track the financial flows underlying AI say that even sharper losses by Nvidia likely wouldn't trigger the kind of systemic problems that regulators guard against. And yet the risks flowing from AI are keeping some finance officials up at night. They are watching for the possibility that many of the factors that have helped the AI boom could reverse simultaneously. If the value of Nvidia's GPU chips fell, for instance, it could prompt investors to ask whether companies that borrowed money to buy them would be able to pay off their debts. In that case, the financial assistance big tech firms have extended to others in the industry could suddenly become drags on their growth. Tech companies would have credit problems at the same time that their equity is falling. Problems among giant tech firms wouldn't stay contained to tech investors' portfolios, but could cause problems across the economy. "I think that's a real concern because both the economy and financial markets are standing on the same leg, which means a drawdown could have reinforcing effects between the two," said Jason Wu, an assistant director at the International Monetary Fund who oversees the Global Markets Analysis unit. Wu was the lead author of a chapter of the IMF's Global Financial Stability report published in October that warned about the potential for growing leverage among AI firms and investors to trigger broader problems. body: So far this year, sovereign yields have risen across the board in the main developed economies, with a particularly sharp increase at longer maturities. Synchronised trends in the US, Europe and Japan point to global forces that go beyond fiscal or institutional factors specific to each country. Although the conflict between the US and Iran has intensified the move, the trend has been evident since late 2024. The nature of this rebound matters because the possible explanations for it have very different economic implications. One interpretation attributes it to higher inflation expectations or a loss of confidence in the sustainability of public finances. Another, particularly in the US, links higher real interest rates to stronger growth prospects stemming from the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) and a possible rise in the neutral interest rate. A third explanation, which lies midway between the two, links greater public and private investment needs to a more price-sensitive investor base that demands higher returns to fund them. Although all three play some role, this latter explanation appears to be the most influential. The rise in long-term interest rates is not primarily driven by higher inflation expectations, although their contribution varies across countries and stages of the conflict. Since the start, real rates have accounted for around 93 of the nearly 100-bp rise in the US 10-year interest rate. Germany and Japan have a more balanced composition, but compensating for inflation, despite gaining importance in recent weeks, is not the main driver of the trend either in the year to date or since the end of 2024. The rise also does not appear to be driven mainly by a widespread crisis of confidence in public finances. The broad-based move affects economies with widely differing fiscal positions and is not confined to those with the most worrying debt trajectories. Switzerland is a notable exception, with a much smaller rebound and a favourable fiscal position. Nevertheless, other economies with sound public finances and no significant deterioration expected, such as Denmark and Norway, have been similarly affected, as they are more exposed to common forces including the European monetary cycle and increased spending needs related to geopolitics and defence. Trends in swap rates confirm that a substantial part of the shift reflects a general rise in the cost of long-term capital, rather than merely a higher sovereign risk premium. Since late February, the rate on the 30-year dollar Overnight Index Swap (OIS) has risen by around 70 bps, compared with around 65 bps for the equivalent Treasury. In the United Kingdom, OIS rates have risen by almost as much as the gilt, while in the euro area the OIS rate has increased by around 30 basis points, some 5 basis points less than the bund . Country-specific fiscal risks do appear to explain differences in the scale of rate increases across countries. France is the clearest example. Alongside the broad rise in long-term interest rates, since early 2023 and amid QT, the spread on 10-year French sovereign debt over the European OIS rate has widened by around 170 bps, compared with some 115 bps against the bund . This reflects both a premium linked to France’s fiscal and political situation and the lower scarcity premium on German debt as the ECB reduces its sovereign bond holdings. Part of the increase reflects expectations that policy rates will remain higher for longer. However, the conflict in Iran and the energy shock have also prompted a sharp repricing at the short end.
